prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Operating and Financial Metrics (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 82px · one-line width 407px
  col 2: header "FY 2022" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 61px
  col 3: header "FY 2023" · longest unbreakable word 62px · one-line width 62px
  col 4: header "FY 2024" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 61px
  col 5: header "Q1 2025" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 63px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"A compact operating and financial KPI table for comparing six metrics across FY 2022, FY 2023, FY 2024 and Q1 2025; readers use it to scan trends over time rather than read prose.","reading":"Scan the first column down to find the metric, then read across the four period columns to compare values. The metric column is the row index; the four period columns form a matched numeric band. Long metric labels will wrap at word boundaries, and period headers can stack as FY / 2022 and Q1 / 2025, but digits and currency/percent tokens should not split.","groups":["Column 1: row-label/index column, separate from all values.","Columns 2–5: one peer group of period-value columns; equal width is appropriate because they play the same role and support across-row comparison. Q1 2025 is a shorter latest period but still belongs to this band."],"keep_intact":["Metric names' unbreakable words such as 'percentage', 'acquisition' and 'recurring' — no mid-word splits","Numeric values including $, commas, decimals and % (e.g. $1,800, 71.3%)","Year digits 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 — headers may break only after 'FY' or 'Q1'"],"may_wrap":["Long metric labels at spaces or commas, over 2–4 lines","Period headers into two lines: FY / 2022, Q1 / 2025","Header rows and metric rows may grow taller; numeric body cells should stay on one line"]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r0A: widths [139, 55, 55, 55, 55] · table 360×650px · row heights [83, 106, 60, 129, 83, 106, 83] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 26
Design r0B: widths [103, 64, 64, 64, 64] · table 360×813px · row heights [60, 153, 83, 153, 106, 129, 129] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 17
Design r0C: widths [103, 82, 82, 82, 82] · table 432×790px · row heights [36, 153, 83, 153, 106, 129, 129] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 2 · OVERFLOWS the box by 72px

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}

log.raw: {"critique":[{"design":"r0A","good":"The metric column is generous (139px), so every row label wraps cleanly at word boundaries in 1–3 lines and the first column reads as a proper row index. '2022' needs ~38px and the widest numeric token ($318.4M, $101.3M) needs ~63px, so both headers and values are forced to split. The 139px given to col 1 was taken out of the columns that hold the data."},{"design":"r0B","good":"Header row is now stable ('FY 2022' etc. on one line) and col 1 at 103px is the true minimum that keeps metric words like 'acquisition' and 'percentage' whole. A table whose latest period is hidden defeats its purpose.","cause":"103px (minimum for whole metric words) + 4×82px (minimum for one-line headers) = 432px, which simply exceeds 359px. Cost: 48px of horizontal scroll — but since any overflow forces the same scroll gesture, spending 48px to remove most numeric splits is a far better trade than r0B's 17 splits for zero scroll."},{"name":"scroll-423","widths":[103,80,80,80,80],"change":"Same reasoning pushed further: 80px gives 59px of text, which absorbs '$402.7M' and '$318.4M'-class values, leaving only the ~63px tokens ($511.9M, $548.2M, $101.3M) broken — about 4 splits for 64px of scroll. Slightly more overflow than scroll-407 for a modest split reduction; offered as the middle point on the split/overflow curve."},{"name":"clean-439","widths":[103,84,84,84,84],"change":"Accept the structural reality that this table cannot fit at 360px and buy a completely clean numeric band: 84px per period column gives 63px of text, enough for every value token including '$318.4M' and '$101.3M' to stay on one line, and headers on one line. 80px overflow is larger than r0C's 72px but r0C's 82px columns still split the two longest figures; this removes them. Choose this only if intact numbers outrank keeping the latest period on screen — otherwise prefer scroll-407."}]}
